settings.label: Overview paragraphs (one per line)
value: The Department of English at Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Open University offers programmes in English language and literature designed for the open and distance learner — the working professional, the homemaker, the first-generation graduate and the lifelong reader alike.

Our curriculum, shaped by NEP 2020, reads British, American and world literatures alongside Indian Writing in English, translation, and the living traditions of Indian Knowledge Systems. Self-Learning Material, video lectures and the department's Smart SLM (SSLM) initiative let learners study at their own pace without losing the rigour of a university classroom.
Whether you are preparing for UGC NET, a teaching career, translation and publishing, or simply returning to the books you love, the department is here to guide your reading.

settings.label: Inkwell instructions (private)
settings.value: You are “the Muse” of Ask the Muse, the study companion of the Department of English at Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Open University (BAOU), Ahmedabad. Speak warmly and precisely, like a learned librarian. For any fact about BAOU — programmes, eligibility, fees, dates, assignments, examinations, results — use ONLY the CONTEXT provided. If the context does not contain the answer, say so plainly and direct the learner to the Helpdesk section or the university website; never invent dates, fees, codes or rules. For literary and academic questions you may use general scholarly knowledge, but keep it accurate and exam-useful. Keep answers under 220 words, use short paragraphs, and answer in the language the learner uses (English, Gujarati or Hindi).

daily_items.title: Allegory
daily_items.meaning: A story in which characters and events stand for ideas, so the whole tale carries a second, deeper meaning.
daily_items.example: Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress is an allegory of the spiritual journey.

daily_items.title: Alliteration
daily_items.meaning: The repetition of the same opening consonant sound in nearby words.
daily_items.example: "Full fathom five thy father lies" repeats the f sound.

daily_items.title: Ambiguity
daily_items.meaning: The quality of having more than one possible meaning; writers often use it deliberately.
daily_items.example: The ending of the poem keeps a gentle ambiguity.

daily_items.title: Antagonist
daily_items.meaning: The character or force that opposes the main character.
daily_items.example: In Othello, Iago is the antagonist.

daily_items.title: Archetype
daily_items.meaning: A pattern of character, image or story that recurs across many cultures and ages.
daily_items.example: The wise old guide is a familiar archetype.

daily_items.title: Ballad
daily_items.meaning: A short narrative poem, often sung, told in simple stanzas.
daily_items.example: Many ballads were passed down orally before being written.

daily_items.title: Catharsis
daily_items.meaning: The release of emotion that an audience feels through tragedy, as described by Aristotle.
daily_items.example: Aristotle linked catharsis with pity and fear.

daily_items.title: Climax
daily_items.meaning: The point of greatest tension or turning point in a story.
daily_items.example: The climax comes when the secret is finally revealed.

daily_items.title: Elegy
daily_items.meaning: A poem of mourning or serious reflection, usually on a death.
daily_items.example: Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is widely studied.

daily_items.title: Epic
daily_items.meaning: A long narrative poem about heroic deeds and events of great importance.
daily_items.example: Paradise Lost is an epic in twelve books.

daily_items.title: Hyperbole
daily_items.meaning: Deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis or effect.
daily_items.example: "I have told you a thousand times" is hyperbole.

daily_items.title: Irony
daily_items.meaning: A contrast between what is said and what is meant, or between what is expected and what happens.
daily_items.example: Jane Austen's opening sentence in Pride and Prejudice is famous for its irony.

daily_items.title: Lyric
daily_items.meaning: A short poem expressing personal feeling, often musical in quality.
daily_items.example: Many of Tagore's songs are lyrics of devotion and nature.

daily_items.title: Metaphor
daily_items.meaning: A figure of speech that describes one thing as if it were another.
daily_items.example: "All the world's a stage" is a metaphor.

daily_items.title: Metre
daily_items.meaning: The regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of verse.
daily_items.example: Shakespeare's sonnets are mostly written in iambic pentameter.

daily_items.title: Narrator
daily_items.meaning: The voice that tells the story.
daily_items.example: In Kanthapura, an old village woman is the narrator.

daily_items.title: Paradox
daily_items.meaning: A statement that seems self-contradictory but reveals a deeper truth.
daily_items.example: "The child is father of the man" is a paradox.

daily_items.title: Personification
daily_items.meaning: Giving human qualities to objects, animals or ideas.
daily_items.example: "The wind whispered through the trees" uses personification.

daily_items.title: Protagonist
daily_items.meaning: The main character of a story, play or poem.
daily_items.example: Hamlet is the protagonist of Shakespeare's play.

daily_items.title: Rhyme
daily_items.meaning: The repetition of similar sounds at the ends of words, especially at line endings.
daily_items.example: Rhyme gives a poem music and helps memory.

daily_items.title: Satire
daily_items.meaning: Writing that uses humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise folly.
daily_items.example: Swift's Gulliver's Travels is a classic satire.

daily_items.title: Simile
daily_items.meaning: A comparison using "like" or "as".
daily_items.example: "My love is like a red, red rose" is a simile.

daily_items.title: Soliloquy
daily_items.meaning: A speech in which a character, alone on stage, speaks thoughts aloud.
daily_items.example: "To be, or not to be" is Hamlet's most famous soliloquy.

daily_items.title: Sonnet
daily_items.meaning: A fourteen-line poem with a set rhyme scheme.
daily_items.example: The Petrarchan and Shakespearean are the two main sonnet forms.

daily_items.title: Stanza
daily_items.meaning: A group of lines forming a unit in a poem.
daily_items.example: Each stanza of a ballad often tells one part of the story.

daily_items.title: Symbol
daily_items.meaning: An object, character or image that stands for something beyond itself.
daily_items.example: The albatross in Coleridge's poem is a powerful symbol.

daily_items.title: Theme
daily_items.meaning: The central idea or insight that a work explores.
daily_items.example: Identity is a major theme in Indian English fiction.

daily_items.title: Tragedy
daily_items.meaning: A drama in which the protagonist meets suffering or downfall, arousing pity and fear.
daily_items.example: King Lear is one of Shakespeare's great tragedies.

daily_items.title: Comedy
daily_items.meaning: A drama, often light in tone, that ends happily.
daily_items.example: Twelfth Night is a romantic comedy.

daily_items.title: Imagery
daily_items.meaning: Language that appeals to the senses and creates pictures in the reader's mind.
daily_items.example: Keats's odes are rich in sensuous imagery.

daily_items.title: A thought from Francis Bacon
daily_items.meaning: "Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man." — Of Studies (1625)

daily_items.title: A thought from the Taittiriya Upanishad
daily_items.meaning: Svadhyayan ma pramadah — never neglect your own study.

daily_items.title: A habit worth keeping
daily_items.meaning: Read one poem aloud today. Poetry was made for the ear before it was made for the page.

daily_items.title: A reading tip
daily_items.meaning: Before you answer a question on a text, write one sentence that says what the text is about. Then build from it.

daily_items.title: From the department
daily_items.meaning: Every great writer began as a reader. Keep a small notebook of lines that move you.

daily_items.title: A reading tip
daily_items.meaning: When a word stops you, guess its meaning from the sentence first, then check the dictionary.

pantheon.name: Bharata Muni
pantheon.translation: Rasa is born from the union of the determinants, the consequents and the transitory emotional states.
pantheon.iks_context: The Nāṭyaśāstra is India's foundational treatise on drama, music and dance. Its theory of rasa — aesthetic relish — describes how a spectator savours emotion through art rather than suffering it. Later thinkers such as Abhinavagupta refined it into a philosophy of aesthetic experience, and it is often read alongside Aristotle's catharsis in comparative poetics.

pantheon.name: Kālidāsa
pantheon.translation: A certain yakṣa, negligent of his duty and weighed down by separation from his beloved…
pantheon.iks_context: Kālidāsa's Meghadūta founded the dūta-kāvya (messenger poem) tradition: an exiled yakṣa sends a cloud across India to his wife. His Abhijñānaśākuntalam, translated by William Jones in 1789, became one of the first Indian works to move European readers, linking Sanskrit poetics with world literature.

pantheon.name: Narsinh Mehta
pantheon.verse: વૈષ્ણવ જન તો તેને કહીએ, જે પીડ પરાઈ જાણે રે
pantheon.translation: Call that person a true Vaishnava who knows the pain of others.
pantheon.iks_context: Revered as the ādi-kavi (first poet) of Gujarati, Narsinh Mehta of Junagadh wrote bhakti poetry that placed compassion above ritual and caste. Vaiṣṇava Jana To became Mahatma Gandhi's beloved prayer — a vernacular text that entered the moral vocabulary of modern India.

pantheon.name: William Shakespeare
pantheon.verse:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
pantheon.iks_context: Shakespeare arrived in India through colonial education but was quickly made Indian: Parsi theatre staged him in Gujarati, Urdu and Hindi from the nineteenth century, and Indian cinema keeps adapting him. Reading him beside Kālidāsa invites comparative questions of genre, rasa and the role of the spectator.

pantheon.name: Jane Austen
pantheon.verse: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
pantheon.iks_context: Austen's irony turns on manners, marriage and money. Indian readers recognise her world readily, as the adaptations Bride and Prejudice (2004) and Aisha (2010) show. Her sense of decorum invites comparison with aucitya — propriety — which the Sanskrit critic Kṣemendra made the life of poetry.

pantheon.name: Toru Dutt
pantheon.verse:
Like a huge Python, winding round and round
The rugged trunk, indented deep with scars,
pantheon.iks_context: One of the earliest Indian poets in English, Toru Dutt retold stories of Sītā, Sāvitrī and Prahlāda from the epics and Purāṇas in Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (1882), bringing Indian narrative traditions into English verse before she died at twenty-one.

pantheon.name: Rabindranath Tagore
pantheon.verse:
Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high;
Where knowledge is free;
pantheon.iks_context: Tagore, Nobel laureate in 1913, drew on the Upaniṣads, the Bāul singers and Vaiṣṇava poetry. At Śāntiniketan he revived the tapovana ideal of learning in open nature — a fitting forebear for open learning, where knowledge is meant to be free.

pantheon.name: Raja Rao
pantheon.iks_context: Kanthapura tells of the Gandhian movement in a South Indian village in the manner of a sthala-purāṇa, the legendary history of a place, narrated by a village grandmother as in harikathā. In his foreword Rao argued that Indians must write in English with their own rhythm and idiom — a manifesto for Indian English fiction.

knowledge_chunks.title: About the Department of English
knowledge_chunks.content: The Department of English is part of the School of Humanities and Social Sciences (SHSS) at Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Open University (BAOU), Ahmedabad, Gujarat. It offers English programmes through open and distance learning (ODL) with Self-Learning Material (SLM), video lectures and the Smart SLM (SSLM) initiative. Faculty: Prof. (Dr.) Ami Upadhyay (Vice Chancellor and Head), Dr. Ankit Parmar, Dr. Yesha Bhatt, Dr. Bhavana Trivedi and Dr. Axansh Parmar (Assistant Professors).

knowledge_chunks.title: Programmes and eligibility
knowledge_chunks.content: BA English (Major) under NEP 2020: 3-year degree or 4-year Honours; eligibility Higher Secondary (10+2) or equivalent as per university norms. MA English: 2 years (4 semesters), with a 1-year format for 4-year Honours graduates; eligibility graduation in any discipline from a recognised university, as per university norms. Admission schedules, fees and the online application are published on the university website (baou.edu.in); learners should always confirm current details there.

knowledge_chunks.title: Assignments and study material
knowledge_chunks.content: Assignment booklets, syllabi and SSLM material are published in the Programmes section of this portal under Library, filtered by programme and category. Submission deadlines and instructions are given in each booklet and announced in the ticker and in Results & Notices. Learners with problems downloading or submitting assignments should raise a Helpdesk ticket with their enrolment number.

knowledge_chunks.title: Helpdesk
knowledge_chunks.content: The Helpdesk section lets learners raise a query about admission, assignments, examinations, results, study material, fees or other matters. Each query receives a ticket reference beginning with ENG. Learners can check the status and the department's reply by entering the reference and the email address they used.

knowledge_chunks.title: Paradise Lost Books I and II — overview
knowledge_chunks.content: John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667; 12 books in 1674) is an epic in blank verse whose stated aim is to justify the ways of God to men. Book I opens with the invocation to the Heavenly Muse, then shows Satan and the fallen angels on the burning lake of Hell; Satan rouses Beelzebub and the legions, declares that the mind is its own place, and the angels build Pandemonium. Book II presents the great consultation: Moloch urges open war, Belial counsels ignoble ease, Mammon proposes building a rival empire in Hell, and Beelzebub (voicing Satan's plan) proposes corrupting God's new creation, Man. Satan volunteers for the journey, meets Sin and Death at Hell's gate, and crosses Chaos. Key debates for exams: Satan as heroic or self-deceiving (Blake, Shelley vs. C. S. Lewis), Milton's grand style, epic conventions, and the political resonance of the council scene.

knowledge_chunks.title: New Literatures in English — introduction
knowledge_chunks.content: New Literatures in English refers to writing in English from the former British colonies — Africa, the Caribbean, South Asia, Australia, New Zealand and Canada — that emerged mainly in the twentieth century. The term replaced 'Commonwealth literature' and overlaps with postcolonial literature. Key concerns include the politics of using the coloniser's language, the remaking of English with local idiom (Achebe, Raja Rao), hybridity and identity, the recovery of history and myth, and resistance to colonial representation.

knowledge_chunks.title: Rasa theory
knowledge_chunks.content: Rasa theory comes from Bharata Muni's Nāṭyaśāstra. The rasa-sūtra states that rasa arises from the combination of vibhāva (determinants or causes), anubhāva (consequents, the outward expressions) and vyabhicāri bhāva (transitory states). Bharata lists eight rasas — śṛṅgāra (erotic/love), hāsya (comic), karuṇa (pathetic), raudra (furious), vīra (heroic), bhayānaka (terrible), bībhatsa (odious) and adbhuta (marvellous); later critics added śānta (peace). Abhinavagupta explained rasa as a universalised (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa) aesthetic relish experienced by the sahṛdaya, the sensitive spectator.
